title: IV. Rebellion
paragraphs: “I have one confession to make,” Ivan began. “I never could understand how anyone can love his neighbors. To my mind, it’s precisely the people close to us that we can’t love. People far away, maybe. I read somewhere about John the Merciful, a saint. A hungry, frozen beggar came to him. The saint took him into his own bed, held him in his arms, and breathed into his mouth, which was putrid and loathsome with some dreadful disease. I’m convinced he did it out of ‘self-laceration,’ the self-laceration of falsity. He did it for the sake of a charity that duty imposed, as a penance laid on him. If you’re to love a man, he has to stay hidden. The moment he shows his face, love is gone.”

“Father Zossima has talked about that more than once,” said Alyosha. “He also said that a man’s face often stands in the way of people who haven’t practiced love. They can’t love him because of it. But there is still a great deal of love among men, almost Christ-like love. I know that myself, Ivan.”

“Well, I don’t know it yet, and I can’t understand it, and the vast mass of mankind is with me on that. The question is whether this comes from men’s bad qualities or from their nature. In my view, Christ-like love for human beings is a miracle that can’t happen on earth. He was God. We are not gods. Say I’m suffering terribly. Nobody else can ever know how much, because he is someone else and not me. And what’s more, people are rarely willing to admit that another person is suffering (as if it were some kind of distinction). Why won’t they, do you think? Because I smell bad, because I have a stupid face, because I once stepped on his foot. And besides, there’s suffering and suffering. The degrading, humiliating kind that brings me low—hunger, for instance—my benefactor may grant me. But when it comes to a higher suffering, for an idea, say, he will very seldom admit it. Maybe my face doesn’t look to him anything like the face he thinks a man should have who suffers for an idea. So he takes back his favor on the spot, and not out of any badness of heart. Beggars, especially genteel beggars, should never show themselves. They should ask for charity through the newspapers. In the abstract, or from a distance, one can love one’s neighbors. Close up, it’s almost impossible. It would be different if it were like the stage, in the ballet, where beggars appear in silk rags and tattered lace and ask for alms while dancing gracefully. Then one might like looking at them. Even so, we wouldn’t love them. But enough of this. I only wanted to give you my point of view. I meant to talk about human suffering in general, but we’d do better to stick to the suffering of children. That shrinks my argument to a tenth of what it could be. Still, let’s keep to the children, although it weakens my case. For one thing, you can love children even close up, even when they’re dirty, even when they’re ugly (though I suspect children are never ugly). My second reason for leaving grown-ups out is this. Besides being disgusting and unworthy of love, they have a compensation. They’ve eaten the apple and know good and evil, and they’ve become ‘like gods.’ They’re still eating it. The children haven’t eaten anything, and so far they’re innocent. Are you fond of children, Alyosha? I know you are, and you’ll see why I prefer to talk about them. If they, too, suffer horribly on earth, then it must be for their fathers’ sins. They must be punished for their fathers, who ate the apple. But that argument belongs to another world, and the human heart here on earth can’t make sense of it. The innocent must not suffer for someone else’s sins, and above all such innocents! It may surprise you, Alyosha, but I’m terribly fond of children, too. And note that cruel people, violent and greedy people, the Karamazovs, are sometimes very fond of children. While children are little, up to seven, say, they’re so far removed from grown-ups. They’re like different creatures, almost another species. I knew a convict in prison who had murdered whole families in his career as a burglar, children among them. Yet in prison he had a strange fondness for children. He spent all his time at his window, watching them play in the prison yard. He taught one little boy to come up to his window and became great friends with him.... You don’t know why I’m telling you all this, Alyosha? My head aches, and I’m sad.”
“You’re talking in a strange way,” Alyosha said uneasily, “as if you weren’t quite yourself.”

“Oh, by the way,” Ivan went on, as though he hadn’t heard his brother, “I met a Bulgarian in Moscow recently. He told me about the atrocities the Turks and Circassians are committing all over Bulgaria. They’re afraid of a general uprising of the Slavs. They burn villages, kill, rape women and children. They nail prisoners to fences by the ears and leave them there until morning, and in the morning they hang them. All sorts of things you can’t imagine. We sometimes speak of bestial cruelty, but that’s a great injustice and an insult to the beasts. No beast can ever be as cruel as a man, so artistically cruel. A tiger only tears and gnaws. That’s all he can do. It would never occur to him to nail people up by the ears, even if he could. These Turks enjoyed torturing children, too. They cut unborn babies out of their mothers’ wombs. They tossed infants into the air and caught them on their bayonets in front of their mothers. Doing it in front of the mothers was what gave the sport its zest. Here is another scene I found very interesting. Picture a trembling mother holding her baby, with a ring of invading Turks around her. They’ve thought up an entertainment. They fuss over the baby and laugh to make it laugh. It works, and the baby laughs. At that moment a Turk aims a pistol four inches from the baby’s face. The baby laughs with delight and reaches out its little hands for the pistol. And he pulls the trigger in the baby’s face and blows out its brains. Artistic, isn’t it? Turks are especially fond of sweets, they say, by the way.”
“Brother, what are you driving at?” asked Alyosha.
“I think that if the devil doesn’t exist, and man made him up, then he made him in his own image and likeness.”
“Just as he did with God, then?” said Alyosha.

“‘It’s wonderful how you can turn words,’ as Polonius says in _Hamlet_,” Ivan laughed. “You turn my own words against me. Well, I’m pleased. A fine God you must have, if man made Him in his own image and likeness. You asked what I was driving at. You see, I like collecting certain facts. Would you believe it, I even copy out anecdotes of a certain sort from newspapers and books, and I already have a fine collection. The Turks are in it, of course, but they’re foreigners. I have specimens from home that are better still. We prefer beating, you know, rods and scourges. That’s our national institution. Nailing people up by the ears is unthinkable for us, because we are Europeans, after all. But the rod and the scourge are always with us, and nobody can take them away. Abroad they hardly do any beating now. Manners are gentler, or laws have been passed, so they don’t dare flog people anymore. But they make up for it in a different way, as national for them as ours is for us. So national that it would hardly be possible here, though I believe we’re being inoculated with it, now that the religious movement has started among our aristocracy. I have a charming pamphlet, translated from the French, about the execution of a murderer named Richard, quite recently, five years ago. He was a young man, I believe twenty-three, who repented and was converted to the Christian faith right at the scaffold. Richard was an illegitimate child. His parents gave him away at the age of six to some shepherds in the Swiss mountains, who raised him to work for them. He grew up among them like a little wild beast. They taught him nothing and barely fed or clothed him. At seven they were sending him out to herd the flock in cold and wet, and nobody hesitated or felt the least scruple about it. Quite the opposite. They thought they had every right, since Richard had been handed over to them like a piece of property. They didn’t even see any need to feed him. Richard himself describes how in those years, like the Prodigal Son in the Gospel, he longed to eat the mash that was given to the pigs, which were being fattened for sale. They wouldn’t give him even that, and they beat him when he stole from the pigs. That’s how he spent his whole childhood and youth. Then he grew up, got strong enough to leave, and became a thief. The savage started earning his living as a day laborer in Geneva. He drank what he earned and lived like a brute. In the end he killed and robbed an old man. He was caught, tried, and sentenced to death. They are not sentimentalists there. In prison he was immediately surrounded by pastors, members of Christian brotherhoods, philanthropic ladies, and so on. They taught him to read and write in prison and explained the Gospel to him. They exhorted him, worked on him, and drummed at him without letup, until at last he solemnly confessed his crime. He was converted. He wrote to the court himself that he was a monster, but that in the end God had granted him light and shown him grace. All Geneva was stirred up about him, all the philanthropic and religious part of it. Everyone of rank and good breeding in the town rushed to the prison to kiss Richard and embrace him. ‘You are our brother, you have found grace.’ And Richard does nothing but weep with emotion. ‘Yes, I’ve found grace! All through my youth and childhood I was glad of pigs’ food, but now even I have found grace. I am dying in the Lord.’ ‘Yes, Richard, die in the Lord. You have shed blood and you must die. It isn’t your fault that you didn’t know the Lord when you coveted the pigs’ food and were beaten for stealing it (which was very wrong of you, for stealing is forbidden). But you have shed blood, and you must die.’ On the last day Richard, completely limp, did nothing but cry and repeat every minute, ‘This is my happiest day. I am going to the Lord.’ ‘Yes,’ cry the pastors and the judges and the philanthropic ladies. ‘This is the happiest day of your life, for you are going to the Lord!’ They all walk or ride to the scaffold in a procession behind the prison van. At the scaffold they call out to Richard, ‘Die, brother, die in the Lord, for even you have found grace!’ And so, covered with his brothers’ kisses, Richard is dragged up onto the scaffold and led to the guillotine. And they cut off his head in a brotherly way, because he had found grace. Yes, that’s characteristic. Some Russian philanthropists of aristocratic rank and evangelical leanings have translated that pamphlet into Russian and given it away free, for the enlightenment of the people. Richard’s case is interesting because it’s so national. To us it’s absurd to cut a man’s head off because he has become our brother and found grace. But we have a specialty of our own, which is almost worse. Our historical pastime is the direct pleasure of inflicting pain. There are lines in Nekrassov about a peasant lashing a horse across the eyes, ‘on its meek eyes.’ Everyone must have seen it. It’s peculiarly Russian. He describes a feeble little nag that has collapsed under too heavy a load and can’t move. The peasant beats it, beats it savagely. At last he beats it without knowing what he’s doing, drunk with cruelty, thrashing it mercilessly again and again. ‘However weak you are, you must pull, even if you die for it.’ The nag strains, and then he starts lashing the poor, defenseless creature across its weeping, its ‘meek eyes.’ The frantic animal tugs and drags the load, trembling all over, gasping, stepping sideways, in a sort of unnatural, convulsive way. It’s awful in Nekrassov. But that’s only a horse, and God gave horses to be beaten. So the Tatars taught us, and they left us the knout to remember it by. But men can be beaten, too. A well-educated, cultured gentleman and his wife beat their own child, a girl of seven, with a birch-rod. I have an exact account of it. The papa was pleased that the birch had twigs all over it. ‘It stings more,’ he said, and so he started stinging his daughter. I know for a fact that there are people who get worked up to sensuality with every blow, literal sensuality, which grows steadily with each blow they deal. They beat for a minute, for five minutes, for ten. They beat more often and more savagely. The child screams. At last the child can’t scream any longer. It gasps, ‘Daddy! daddy!’ By some diabolical, unseemly chance the case came to court. A lawyer is hired. The Russian people have long called a barrister ‘a conscience for hire.’ The lawyer speaks up in his client’s defense. ‘It’s such a simple thing,’ he says, ‘an everyday matter within the family. A father corrects his child. To our shame, it has been brought into court.’ The jury, won over by him, returns a favorable verdict. The public roars with delight that the torturer has been acquitted. Ah, what a pity I wasn’t there! I would have proposed starting a subscription in his honor! Charming pictures.

“But I have better things still about children. I’ve collected a great, great deal about Russian children, Alyosha. There was a little girl of five whose father and mother hated her, ‘most worthy and respectable people, of good education and breeding.’ You see, I have to say it again: it’s a peculiar trait of many people, this love of torturing children, and only children. With every other kind of person these torturers are mild and kindly, like cultivated, humane Europeans. But they love to torment children. In that sense they even love the children themselves. It’s precisely the child’s defenselessness that tempts the tormentor. It’s the angelic trust of a child with no refuge and no one to appeal to that sets his vile blood on fire. In every man, of course, a demon lies hidden: the demon of rage, the demon of lustful heat at the screams of the tortured victim, the demon of lawlessness let off its chain, the demon of the diseases that follow vice, gout, kidney disease, and so on.

“Those cultivated parents put this poor five-year-old through every torture imaginable. They beat her, thrashed her, kicked her for no reason, until her whole body was one bruise. Then they got more refined in their cruelty. They locked her up all night in an outhouse, in the cold and frost. And because she hadn’t asked to be taken out in the night (as if a five-year-old, sleeping her sound, angelic sleep, could be trained to wake and ask!), they smeared her face with excrement and filled her mouth with it, and it was her mother, her own mother, who did this. And that mother could sleep while she heard the poor child groaning! Can you understand why a little creature, who can’t even grasp what is being done to her, should beat her aching little heart with her tiny fist in the dark and the cold, and weep her meek, unresentful tears to ‘dear, kind God’ to protect her? Do you understand that, my friend and brother, you pious, humble novice? Do you understand why this infamy has to exist and is allowed to? I’m told that without it man couldn’t have lived on earth, since he wouldn’t have known good and evil. Why should he know that diabolical good and evil, when it costs so much? The whole world of knowledge isn’t worth that child’s prayer to ‘dear, kind God’! I say nothing about the suffering of grown-up people. They ate the apple, damn them, and the devil take them all! But these little ones! I’m making you suffer, Alyosha. You’re not yourself. I’ll stop if you like.”
“Never mind. I want to suffer too,” muttered Alyosha.

“One more picture, just one, because it’s so curious and so typical. I only just read it in some collection of Russian antiquities, and I’ve forgotten the name. I’ll have to look it up. It happened in the darkest days of serfdom, early in the century, and long live the Liberator of the People! In those days there was a general with aristocratic connections who owned great estates. He was one of those men (somewhat exceptional even then, I believe) who retire from the service into a life of leisure, convinced that it has earned them absolute power over the lives of their subjects. There were such men then. So this general settled on his estate of two thousand souls and lived in grand style, lording it over his poor neighbors as if they were hangers-on and jesters. He had kennels with hundreds of hounds and nearly a hundred dog-boys, all in uniform and all mounted. One day a serf-boy, a little child of eight, threw a stone in play and hurt the paw of the general’s favorite hound. ‘Why is my favorite dog lame?’ He is told that the boy threw a stone and hurt its paw. ‘So you did it.’ The general looked the child up and down. ‘Take him.’ They took him. They took him from his mother and kept him locked up all night. Early the next morning the general rides out in full hunting parade, with his hounds, his dependents, dog-boys and huntsmen, all mounted around him. The servants are summoned to be edified, and in front of them all stands the child’s mother. The child is brought out of the lock-up. It’s a gloomy, cold, foggy autumn day, a capital day for hunting. The general orders the child undressed. The boy is stripped naked. He shivers, numb with terror, not daring to cry.... ‘Make him run,’ commands the general. ‘Run! Run!’ shout the dog-boys. The boy runs.... ‘At him!’ yells the general, and he looses the whole pack on the child. The hounds seize him and tear him to pieces before his mother’s eyes!... I believe the general was later declared unfit to run his estates. Well, what did he deserve? To be shot? To be shot, to satisfy our moral feelings? Speak, Alyosha!”
“To be shot,” Alyosha murmured, looking up at Ivan with a pale, crooked smile.
“Bravo!” cried Ivan, delighted. “If even you say so.... Some monk you are! So there’s a little devil sitting in your heart, Alyosha Karamazov!”
“What I said was absurd, but—”

“That’s exactly it, that ‘but’!” cried Ivan. “I’ll tell you something, novice: the absurd is only too necessary on earth. The world stands on absurdities, and maybe nothing at all would have happened in it without them. We know what we know!”
“What do you know?”

“I understand nothing,” Ivan went on, as if in delirium. “I don’t want to understand anything now. I want to stay with the fact. I decided long ago not to understand. If I start trying to understand something, I’ll betray the fact, and I’m determined to stay with the fact.”
“Why are you testing me?” Alyosha cried, in sudden distress. “Are you going to tell me what you mean, at last?”
“Of course I am. That’s what I’ve been working up to. You’re dear to me. I don’t want to let you go, and I won’t give you up to your Zossima.”
Ivan was silent for a minute, and all at once his face turned very sad.

“Listen! I took up the case of children only to make my point clearer. As for the other tears of humanity, which soak the earth from its crust to its core, I’ll say nothing about them. I’ve narrowed my subject on purpose. I’m a bug, and I admit in all humility that I can’t understand why the world is arranged the way it is. Men are to blame themselves, I suppose. They were given paradise, they wanted freedom, and they stole fire from heaven, knowing they would be made unhappy. So there’s no need to pity them. All I know, with my pitiful, earthly, Euclidian mind, is that there is suffering and nobody is guilty; that cause follows effect plainly and directly; that everything flows and finds its level. But that’s only Euclidian nonsense, I know it, and I can’t agree to live by it! What comfort is it to me that nobody is guilty, that cause follows effect plainly and directly, and that I know it? I must have justice, or I’ll destroy myself. And not justice in some remote, infinite time and place, but here on earth, where I can see it myself. I have believed in it. I want to see it, and if I’m dead by then, let me rise again. If it all happens without me, that will be too unfair. Surely I didn’t suffer just so that my crimes and my sufferings could manure the ground for somebody else’s future harmony. I want to see with my own eyes the hind lie down with the lion, and the victim rise up and embrace his murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly understands what it was all for. Every religion in the world is built on this longing, and I am a believer. But then there are the children, and what am I to do about them? That’s the question I can’t answer. For the hundredth time I say it: there are masses of questions, but I’ve taken only the children, because in their case what I mean is unanswerably clear. Listen! If everyone has to suffer in order to pay for the eternal harmony, what do children have to do with it? Tell me, please. It’s beyond all understanding why they should suffer, and why they should have to pay for the harmony. Why should they, too, be material to enrich the soil for somebody’s future harmony? I understand solidarity among men in sin. I understand solidarity in retribution, too. But there can be no such solidarity with children. And if it’s really true that they share the responsibility for all their fathers’ crimes, then that truth does not belong to this world, and I can’t comprehend it. Some jester will say, perhaps, that the child would have grown up and sinned. But he didn’t grow up, you see. He was torn to pieces by dogs at eight years old. Oh, Alyosha, I’m not blaspheming! I do understand what an upheaval of the universe it will be, when everything in heaven and on earth blends into one hymn of praise, and everything that lives and has lived cries aloud: ‘You are just, O Lord, for Your ways are revealed.’ When the mother embraces the fiend who threw her child to the dogs, and all three cry aloud through their tears, ‘You are just, O Lord!’ then, of course, the crown of knowledge will have been reached and everything will be clear. But this is exactly where I stop: I can’t accept that harmony. And while I’m still on earth, I make haste to take my own measures. You see, Alyosha, perhaps it really may happen that if I live to see that moment, or rise again to witness it, I too, perhaps, may cry out with the rest, as I watch the mother embrace her child’s torturer, ‘You are just, O Lord!’ But I don’t want to cry it out then. While there’s still time, I hurry to protect myself, and so I renounce the higher harmony altogether. It isn’t worth the tears of that one tortured child, who beat her little chest with her little fist and prayed in her stinking outhouse, with her unatoned tears, to ‘dear, kind God’! It isn’t worth it, because those tears are unatoned for. They have to be atoned for, or there can be no harmony. But how? How will you atone for them? Is it even possible? By avenging them? But what do I care about avenging them? What do I care about a hell for the oppressors? What good can hell do, when those children have already been tortured? And what becomes of harmony, if there is a hell? I want to forgive. I want to embrace. I don’t want any more suffering. And if the suffering of children goes to make up the sum of suffering needed to pay for the truth, then I protest that the truth isn’t worth such a price. I don’t want the mother to embrace the oppressor who threw her son to the dogs! She has no right to forgive him! Let her forgive him for herself, if she wants to. Let her forgive the torturer for the immeasurable suffering of her own mother’s heart. But the suffering of her tortured child she has no right to forgive. She must not forgive the torturer, even if the child forgave him! And if that’s so, if they have no right to forgive, what becomes of harmony? Is there anyone in the whole world who would have the right to forgive, and could? I don’t want harmony. Out of love for humanity I don’t want it. I’d rather keep my unavenged suffering. I’d rather stay with my unavenged suffering and my unsatisfied indignation, _even if I were wrong_. Besides, the price of harmony is too high. It’s beyond our means to pay so much to get in. And so I hurry to hand back my entrance ticket, and if I’m an honest man, I’m bound to hand it back as soon as I can. That’s what I’m doing. It isn’t God I don’t accept, Alyosha. I just most respectfully return Him the ticket.”
“That’s rebellion,” murmured Alyosha, looking down.

“Rebellion? I’m sorry you call it that,” said Ivan earnestly. “One can hardly live in rebellion, and I want to live. Tell me yourself, I challenge you, answer. Suppose you were building the fabric of human destiny, with the aim of making people happy in the end and giving them peace and rest at last. But suppose it was essential and unavoidable to torture to death just one tiny creature, that baby beating her chest with her fist, for example, and to build that edifice on her unavenged tears. Would you agree to be the architect on those terms? Tell me, and tell the truth.”
“No, I wouldn’t agree,” said Alyosha softly.

“And can you accept that the people you were building it for would consent to take their happiness on the foundation of a little victim’s unatoned blood? And that, having taken it, they would stay happy for ever?”

“No, I can’t accept that. Brother,” said Alyosha suddenly, his eyes flashing, “you just asked whether there is a being in the whole world who would have the right to forgive, and could. But there is a Being, and He can forgive everything, all and for all, because He gave His innocent blood for all and for everything. You’ve forgotten Him, and the edifice is built on Him, and it is to Him they cry aloud, ‘You are just, O Lord, for Your ways are revealed!’”

“Ah! The One without sin, and His blood! No, I haven’t forgotten Him. On the contrary, I’ve been wondering the whole time why you hadn’t brought Him in sooner, since in arguments on your side He usually comes first. Do you know, Alyosha, and don’t laugh, I composed a poem about a year ago. If you can waste another ten minutes on me, I’ll tell it to you.”
“You wrote a poem?”

“Oh, no, I didn’t write it,” laughed Ivan. “I’ve never written two lines of verse in my life. But I made up this poem, in prose, and I remembered it. I got carried away when I made it up. You’ll be my first reader, or rather listener. Why should an author give up even one listener?” smiled Ivan. “Shall I tell it to you?”
“I’m listening,” said Alyosha.
“The poem’s title is ‘The Grand Inquisitor.’ It’s a ridiculous piece of work, but I want to tell it to you.”
